title: The solid rock
hookLine: as a solid rock isn't shaken by wind, the wise aren't moved by praise or blame (Dhammapada 81)
tomorrow: Zoe's drafted a very long text to Theo. send it, or not?

lines: THE PHONE AS A WEATHER VANE.
cards: Post something you care about, and the phone becomes a weather vane. A kind comment, and the day lifts. One sharp one, and it sinks.
Which knocks you over faster, praise or blame? The Dhammapada says it's the same wind.
Verse eighty-one, in Max Müller's translation: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." Blame and praise, in one breath.

teach.h: ONE ROAD: A CRITIC AND A FAN.
teach.b: The Buddha walked through that wind himself. At the opening of the Brahmajala Sutta, in the Long Discourses, he's on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda with his monks.
Behind them walks a wanderer named Suppiya with his own student, Brahmadatta. The whole way, the teacher speaks against the Buddha and his teaching, and the student speaks in praise of them.
Blame and praise, side by side, on one road. Next morning the monks talk it over.
The Buddha tells them: if others speak against me, don't be angry. If others speak in praise, don't be elated. In both cases, look at what's actually true and what isn't.
Buddhists count praise and blame among the eight worldly conditions, with gain and loss, fame and disrepute, pleasure and pain.
They come and go for everyone. Steadiness among them is called equanimity, and it's trained, not born.
A rock isn't hard because it ignores the wind. It's heavy, and low, and the wind has nothing to grip.

how: Buddhist teachers name praise and blame among the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma); equanimity toward them is cultivated in meditation and in daily life.

o: hard-hearted, so nothing anyone says gets in
stubborn, never willing to change your mind
steady when praised and when blamed, like a rock

games.q: the road and the rock: tap the pairs.
p: the teacher who spoke against the Buddha
the student who spoke in praise
gain, loss, fame, disrepute, praise, blame…

s: the verse only warns about blame; praise is safe
blame and praise, in one breath: the same wind.
the Buddha told his monks not to be elated when others praised him
not angry at blame, not elated at praise: look at what's true.
equanimity means not caring what anyone says
the Buddha said to check what's true in both; steady isn't the same as deaf.

games.q: you're one of the monks. all day a teacher behind you blamed the Buddha and his student praised him. what does the Buddha tell you the next morning?
o: defend the teaching against the critic, and thank the student.
don't be angry at the blame or elated at the praise; check what's true.
ignore them both; outsiders can't understand the teaching.
games.why: neither anger nor elation. he told them to look at what was actually true in what was said.

practice: Sit low and let your weight sink, feet flat, one hand resting on something solid: the floor, a table, a stone if you have one. Feel how heavy you are.
Let the breath move like wind across the surface while the weight stays where it is. If a comment from today comes to mind, praise or blame, let it pass over like weather.

wordCard.voice: The solid rock: the wise, unshaken by blame and unlifted by praise, the way a rock stays put in the wind.

orig.note: Pali, written in Devanagari: sela, rock. verse 81 opens selo yatha ekaghano, like a solid rock.

carryVoice: Your line: the solid rock, steady in praise and in blame. Four verses down, and the wind keeps blowing.

sources.q: As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta 1.1–1.6 (Suppiya and Brahmadatta on the road; not angry at dispraise, not elated at praise; check what is true)
sources.work: Dialogues of the Buddha, part I

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 8.6 (the eight worldly conditions: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain)
